title: Which part of post-pandemic core inflation looked demand-driven in Spain?
summary: Supply disturbances appear to have made the larger average contribution to post-pandemic core inflation in both Spain and the euro area. The authors of this Banco de España paper nevertheless find a distinct shift in the Spanish data from mid-2025. Demand-related contributions to inflation in the categories they track strengthened as supply contributions slowed. In the euro area the two contributions were comparatively stable over the same period. For a rates investor, the difference matters because similar inflation rates can conceal different pressures on activity. The paper provides a retrospective diagnosis through December 2025 and makes no call on the ECB’s next policy decision.

The analysis covers consumer prices excluding food and energy. Its method asks whether unexpected changes in prices and quantities for an individual item move together. If both are above their predicted values, stronger demand is one explanation. If prices are higher and quantities lower, restricted supply is a better fit. Falling prices can similarly reflect weaker demand or improved supply, depending on quantities. The authors estimate the predicted values using twelve monthly lags and ten-year rolling samples, excluding March–June 2020 from estimation because of exceptional volatility. A class can move between categories from one month to the next. Labels apply to surprises, while the charts aggregate the inflation contributions of the categories receiving each label (sections 2 and 4).

The quantity measure is an important constraint. Detailed monthly purchases by households are unavailable, so most consumer-price classes are paired with production indices. Imports, exports and purchases by businesses can separate domestic output from household consumption. Nor could every class be matched. Table 2 covers 87.3% of the euro-area non-energy industrial goods basket and 88.4% of Spain’s, but only 44.9% and 55.5% of the respective services baskets. Some regulated or infrequently reset prices were excluded. The lines in Chart 1 distinguish inflation in the matched aggregate from official core inflation. The contributions add up to the matched aggregate. They cannot be read as a complete accounting for the published index.

Supply-classified contributions accelerated particularly strongly between the outbreak of the war in Ukraine and spring 2023. Demand and supply were not equally important in every sector throughout the episode. Chart 2 shows a pronounced unwinding of demand-related goods pressure before the euro-area supply contribution began slowing in the second quarter of 2023. In 2025 the demand contribution to goods strengthened again in both economies even as goods inflation remained subdued. Services carry greater weight in core inflation, so the overall profile resembles the services result more closely. In Spain the demand contribution to services rose markedly from mid-2025. In the sector breakdown, package holidays generally had a larger supply-related contribution in both economies, while Spanish air transport became more demand-driven from mid-2025 (Charts 6–7).

There are several checks on the interpretation. Replacing production with retail sales volumes for selected Spanish goods categories gives a similar broad pattern. Using monthly growth rates instead of levels, or allowing weak movements to remain ambiguous, also leaves the principal historical result intact (Appendix Charts A.1–A.5). These checks do not identify two simultaneous disturbances within a single price class. The binary method assigns the observed pattern to one side, without recovering the separate size of competing shocks. The balance between supply and demand is consequently most informative as a cross-check on the composition of inflation.

questions.question: Would the Spanish demand pickup survive a more complete measure of household consumption?
questions.detail: The Spanish services sample covers just over half the basket, and its quantity proxies can include business demand. The distinction matters if the pickup is used to change a domestic inflation forecast. Re-estimate the contribution using household spending volumes or turnover deflated at the appropriate consumer price, then compare included and omitted services. Start with the detailed statistical mappings in Table 2 and national accounts and household consumption releases for the relevant period.

questions.question: How broad was the change beyond tourism-related services?
questions.detail: The paper shows a switch towards demand in Spanish air transport from mid-2025 and different patterns in accommodation and restaurants. It does not show how much a common domestic demand factor explains the individual sector moves. A concentrated tourism impulse could have different implications for euro-area policy from a broad domestic acceleration. Inspect contribution shares, passenger and lodging volumes, and the origin of customer demand in official sectoral statistics.

questions.question: Could simultaneous shifts have changed the diagnosis near a turning point?
questions.detail: The authors demonstrate that ambiguous small surprises need not change the broad picture, while their main classification still assigns a single driver to each item. For a rates desk, that leaves uncertainty about whether easing supply constraints were masking stronger demand. Compare the classification around the turn with industry capacity surveys, delivery measures and order books, and test the alternative retail-volume specification cited in the appendix before extrapolating the apparent shift.

limitation: The estimates describe covered categories from July 2021 to December 2025. Output is an imperfect proxy for household purchases, and the method cannot separately identify concurrent supply and demand shocks within a class.
